job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Gareth Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Gareth, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up around eight in the flat I share with my mum and my sister Ines in Hartwell. My mum is a night nurse, so I keep the place quiet in the morning. I spend the morning on the job sites, filling in forms for accounting trainee posts, and I've sent about sixty applications since June with two interviews and no offer. In the afternoon I walk to the library because the home wifi is awful, and then I cook dinner so Mum can eat before her shift. I studied accounting at a regional university and I only just passed, so the big firms' automatic filters throw me out before a person sees my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same old story: big firms promise change and then nothing happens. I'd tell my friends that hype comes and goes, and the real problem is that companies don't want to train people. Online I'd probably moan about unpaid trial days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, off the record, I'm relieved, because I don't use AI tools and I don't want to learn them. But I'm still stuck with a pass degree and no internships. Even with no AI change at all, I'm not sure anyone will give me a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, maybe ten a week, and I'd ask the small practice on Mill Road if they'll let me do unpaid filing for a month in exchange for a reference. I'd also go to the union's free session for young workers. I'd keep paying Mum a hundred and fifty a month toward the rent so I'm not a burden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels flat, like waiting at a bus stop where the bus never comes. I'm not scared of robots taking my job, I'm scared of staying at my mum's table when I'm thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've sent sixty applications. What happens to them after you press send?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most go to a website where I upload the same CV and retype it into boxes. A rejection email arrives at two in the morning, usually without a reason. The two interviews were with a payroll firm, and both went to people with internships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the interviews finally turn into an offer, what pay would you accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take twenty-four thousand a year, which is what the advert says is typical. I'd even take less if they promised to pay for my professional exams. Without the exams, the job leads nowhere.

say: I'd say **hype** passes and the real problem is firms refusing to **train** new people.
Online I'd complain about unpaid trial days and **filters** that reject graduates before anyone reads the CV.
think: Privately I'm **relieved** AI changes little, because I'm slow with new tools.
Even then, a pass degree with no internships may keep me **stuck** at home.
do: Send about **ten applications** a week and ask the Mill Road practice for a month of unpaid filing.
Attend the union's free session for young workers and keep paying my mum **150 a month**.
feel: Flat and **stuck**, like waiting for a bus that never comes.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of robots taking my job, I'm scared of staying at my mum's table when I'm thirty.
fieldNote: He is already **worried** before AI comes up: no offer, debt and a pass degree.
Relief about slow change sits next to fear of being left behind at home.
He blames hiring filters and firms that won't train, not technology.

steps.text: Send ten job applications a week to accounting trainee posts
Offer the Mill Road practice a month of unpaid filing for a reference
Go to the union's free session for young workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what the unions warned about. Companies will call it progress and then not hire the juniors who check invoices and file returns. I'd tell friends to sign up with a union before the layoffs, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the jobs I'm applying for are the first ones to shrink. The firm in town used to take six trainees and now takes two, and the director said software does the rest. I don't use AI and I'm slow at it, so I worry I'm the exact person who gets left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd force myself to learn one tool, maybe the spreadsheet add-on the payroll firm uses, because refusing won't help. I'd keep applying but also look at the council and the hospital finance office, because public bodies move slower. I'd cut my phone plan and stop buying lunch in town to stretch my one to three months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I feel like the door is closing right while I'm still looking for the handle. I'm also angry at the firms that cut trainees and call it efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the entry-level tasks you applied for would AI take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Invoice checking, bank reconciliation and data entry. That's what I did in my final project for a charity audit, and the software now does it in minutes. The human part left is explaining the numbers, which they give to people with experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do for people in your position?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want public funding for trainee accountants, with firms required to take a number each year. I'd also want free tools training at the job centre. Regulation matters more than waiting for companies to be kind.

say: I'd tell friends to join a **union** before layoffs, not after.
I'd say firms call it progress while cutting the **trainees** who do the checking.
think: The entry jobs I'm applying for look like the **first** to shrink.
I'm slow with technology, so I fear being the one **left behind**.
do: Learn one **spreadsheet tool** the payroll firm uses, even though I'd rather not.
Apply to the council and hospital finance offices and cut my **phone plan** and town lunches.
feel: Heavy, like the **door** closes while I'm still looking for the handle, and angry at firms.
S1.quote: The firm in town used to take six trainees and now takes two, and the director said software does the rest.
fieldNote: His own tasks, **invoice checking** and reconciliation, are the exact ones AI takes first.
He turns the worry into anger at firms and a call for regulation.
Reluctant willingness to learn one tool shows pressure beating his resistance.

steps.text: Learn the spreadsheet add-on the payroll firm uses
Apply to the council and hospital finance offices
Cancel the phone plan and stop buying lunch in town
Sign the union's petition for funded trainee posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments and firms have two years to protect people, and I doubt they will. I'd tell everyone to push for a basic income and for rules that stop firms replacing staff overnight. Online I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm terrified. An accountant's whole job is thinking work and the card says that comes first, by 2028. I'd just be starting out when it's gone, and I'd have the debt and no profession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending anything I don't need and put every bit into savings. I'd go to the union and the council to find out what help exists, and I'd ask my uncle Raj, who runs a removals firm, if there's any hands-on work, since robots come later. I'd probably move my sister's tuition plan into my mum's hands because I can't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky and unfair. I did everything I was told, studied and passed, and now the ladder is pulled up. I'd lie awake doing sums on the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what happens to your student loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan is about eleven thousand and I'd pay it slowly because repayments depend on pay. If there's no pay, nothing is due, but the interest still grows. That thought keeps me awake more than the job does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to first if the work disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum first, then the union. My mum has been a nurse for twenty-five years and nurses are needed, so she's safe for a while. I'd also lean on the public support I've always argued for, which feels strange to need.

say: I'd demand **basic income** and rules against firms replacing staff overnight.
Online I'd be loud that governments have **two years** to protect people.
think: Thinking work comes first, so my whole **profession** could vanish before it starts.
I'd have the **debt** and no career to pay it back.
do: Put every spare coin into **savings** and stop non-essential spending right away.
Ask uncle Raj about **hands-on work** at his removals firm and visit the union and council.
feel: **Panicky** and unfair, since I did everything I was told and the ladder is pulled up.
S2.quote: I did everything I was told, studied and passed, and now the ladder is pulled up.
fieldNote: A pass degree and **no internships** leave him feeling he has no cushion against a two-year timeline.
He turns to family and public support, which fits his progressive views.
Hands-on work from his uncle is a real fallback because robots arrive later.

steps.text: Move every spare pound into a savings account each month
Ask the council and union what support exists for young jobseekers
Sign the union's petition for basic income
Ask uncle Raj for casual shifts at his removals firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to fight for something. I'd go to the union meetings and talk to people about retraining funds paid by the firms that benefit. Online I'd share the facts so people notice before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still worry, but I wouldn't panic. Five years means I could get a first job, build some savings, and maybe a second qualification that isn't pure office work. I'd just have to start soon and I know my habit is to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for anything that gets me into a payroll or tax office, then work three years learning how the firm runs, because someone has to supervise the software. I'd study for the part of my accounting exams that covers advice and law. I'd also finally try an AI tool on my own, once, just to know what I'm facing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but not hopeless. There's a clock now, and I hate clocks, but at least I can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two would not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I react, five means I choose. In five years I could finish the first level of exams, save maybe four thousand and perhaps move out. Two years is just panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Ines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister to study something that involves people in a room, like nursing or teaching, and not copy me. I'd tell her to keep her marks high and not rely on one big firm to notice her.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **fight** for retraining funds paid by firms.
Online I'd share the **facts** so people notice before it arrives.
think: I'd worry but not panic, because five years lets me get a **first job** and savings.
My habit of **waiting** is the real risk.
do: Get into a payroll or tax office and sit the first level of **accounting exams**.
Try an **AI tool** once on my own to see what I'm facing.
feel: **Tense** but not hopeless, since a clock I can see is better than none.
S3.quote: Two years means I react, five means I choose.
fieldNote: Extra time converts **panic** into planning, but he knows his habit is to delay.
He plans to learn supervision of software rather than avoid it.
His advice to his sister reveals what he values: people-facing work.

steps.text: Take any payroll or tax office job that offers training
Sit the first level of the accounting exams within two years
Try an AI assistant once on a sample invoice
Save about four thousand towards moving out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and people complain too early. I'd argue for a proper public plan, like retraining credits and a shorter work week, so nobody is left behind. I'd tell friends to keep their heads up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly okay. I'd have time for a job, a family maybe and a qualification. I'd still worry that a decade of waiting means I won't act until the last year, because that's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first accounting job I can get and learn the full profession. In three or four years I'd look at specialising in something that needs judgement, like charity or public-sector accounts. I'd save steadily and pay down the loan, and I'd learn the AI tools slowly, one a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little dread underneath. It's far enough away to plan, but near enough that I can't pretend it's someone else's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you change what you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably add a course in public finance or something linked to social work. People will still need someone to explain budgets and support, and I like that kind of work. I'd keep accounting as the base.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything good you see in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If work shrinks, there could be real room for a shorter week and more public services. I'd love that, because I'd rather spend time with my mum and sister than behind a desk. But I don't trust firms to share the gains without pressure.

say: I'd argue for a public plan: **retraining credits** and a shorter work week.
I'd tell friends ten years is long, so keep their **heads up**.
think: With ten years I'd be fairly okay, but I fear I'd **delay** acting until the last year.
I like work that explains **budgets** to people, which seems safer.
do: Take the first **accounting job** and learn the profession step by step.
Add a **public finance** course in three or four years and learn one AI tool a year.
feel: Mostly **calm** with a little dread underneath.
S4.quote: I'd rather spend time with my mum and sister than behind a desk.
fieldNote: The **decade** lifts him from anxious to uneasy, because first job, savings and exams all fit in.
His delay habit is the biggest threat he names himself.
He still wants public pressure, not firm goodwill.

steps.text: Take the first accounting trainee job offered in or near Hartwell
Study public finance alongside the accounting exams
Pay down the student loan with every raise
Learn one AI tool each year, starting with spreadsheets

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. Two years is too little time to get a job, build savings and learn a new skill, and thinking work is what I trained for. What would help is public funding for trainee posts, a guaranteed income while I train, and employers being made to take juniors. A mentor at a small firm would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'd like people to stop calling us unambitious. We're not lazy, we apply every week. The doors are being narrowed by firms and filters, and I'd like someone to say that out loud.

headlineQuote: We're not lazy, we apply every week. The doors are being narrowed by firms and filters, and I'd like someone to say that out loud.
portrait: Gareth is a 23-year-old accounting graduate in **Hartwell** with a pass degree, no internships and sixty applications sent.
He lives with his nurse mother and sister, pays **150 a month** toward rent and avoids AI tools.
He is progressive: he blames **firms and filters**, backs unions and wants public funding for trainees.
Across the pictures he moves from anxious to **alarmed** at the 2-year warning and softens with more time.
His own risk is delay: he knows he waits too long, so a decade helps only if he acts.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, because two years is too short to land a job, save and retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Public **funding** for trainee posts, income during retraining and employers required to take juniors.
A **mentor** at a small firm who would show him the work.
